title: Nakamura Bounces Back To Win 73rd Bullet Brawl Title, Gurel Finishes 2nd
summary:
GM Hikaru Nakamura wasted little time reclaiming his place at the top of the Bullet Brawl standings, capturing his 73rd title after finishing ahead of GM Ediz Gurel and GM Parham Maghsoodloo in Saturday's 225-player arena.

Nakamura scored 165 points, 12 more than Gurel's 153, while Maghsoodloo took third with 141. GM Faustino Oro narrowly missed the podium, finishing just one point behind the Iranian grandmaster, while IM Karina Ambartsumova picked up the $100 best women's prize.

The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, November 14, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CET / 10:30 p.m. IST.

Of the 12 participants rated 3200 or higher who vied for victory in Saturday's Bullet Brawl, it was Gurel who had the finest start. The 17-year-old Turkish GM scored 26.5/30 in the first hour of the event and dispatched the likes of GMs Oleksandr Bortnyk, Rasmus Svane, Oro, his compatriot Yagiz Erdogmus, and Nakamura himself.

Gurel scored more points in the first half than most of the field scored in the entire event. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Chess.com.

Gurel's tactical acumen came to the fore on multiple occasions. in his clash with fellow prodigy Oro, Gurel highlighted his opponent's overextension with a clever tactic that won a pawn and consolidated his advantage. Can you work out the cunning plan below?

One of Gurel's best wins came against Nakamura, after the latter slipped with 33...Nd2?? having played almost flawlessly in the opening and middlegame. Gurel's accuracy rating in the game, according to Game Review, is a remarkable 98.8%.

By all accounts, Nakamura's declaration in the third quarter that he was having a "rough event" was justified when compared with his recent domination. Nevertheless, the American managed to stay within striking range of Gurel as the arena entered its final stages.

Nakamura's journey to the top was a rollercoaster on Saturday. Image: GMHikaru/Kick.

Perhaps inspired by GM Alireza Firouzja's comeback victory in the previous edition, Nakamura mounted a late charge as Gurel began to falter. The world number-two scored 2.5/3 against Gurel during a nine-game streak that saw him creep to within three points of the leader.

A subsequent six-game winning streak saw Nakamura tighten the screws. Wins over GMs Dmitry Andreikin, Bortnyk (twice), Gurel (twice), as well as IM Sergey Sklokin propelled him past Gurel and into the lead, leaving other challengers, Maghsoodloo and Oro, trailing behind.

Nakamura burst Gurel's bubble in the final quarter.

In their final matchup, Nakamura had to weather Gurel's brilliant 29.Nxg5!! before he could eventually turn the tables and secure his 73rd Bullet Brawl title.

title: FIDE World Senior Championships 2026: Six rounds left, four titles at stake
summary: Five rounds have been played at the FIDE World Senior Chess Championships 2026 in Vrnjačka Banja, Serbia, and the competition is taking shape across all four categories. Some of the pre-tournament favourites are living up to expectations, while others have already dropped valuable points. With six rounds still to come, there is plenty of chess left to play. The standout performance of the first five rounds belongs to WGM Galina Strutinskaya, the only player in the event with a perfect score. Women 65+: Strutinskaya remains perfect WGM Galina Strutinskaya (FIDE) could hardly have asked for a better start. Five games, five victories and a full-point lead over her nearest rivals. WGM Irina Chelushkina (Serbia) and WIM Larisa Khropova (FIDE) share second place with 4/5. Three players are another half-point behind: Elena Krasenkowa (Poland), Bagyashree Sathe Thipsay (India), and Ingrid Lauterbach (Germany).  Among the participants is one of the greatest figures in chess history, former Women’s World Champion GM Nona Gaprindashvili of Georgia. The top seed, who is also competing for the special Women 75+ title, has collected three points from five games. Despite a modest start by her standards, her experience and competitive spirit make her a player to watch in the remaining rounds. Strutinskaya has put herself in an excellent position, but with six rounds remaining, her closest rivals still have time to challenge her lead. Standings after Round 5 Women 50+: Calzetta Ruiz leads ahead of Cramling Spain’s WGM Monica Calzetta Ruiz leads the Women 50+ championship with 4.5 points from five games, half a point ahead of Swedish GM Pia Cramling. Cramling, the top seed and one of the most respected players in women’s chess, remains unbeaten on four points. She is well placed to challenge for the title, although there is no shortage of competition behind her. Six players are tied on 3.5 points: IM Inna Gaponenko (Ukraine), WGM Maritza Arribas Robaina (Cuba), WIM Sopio Tereladze and WGM Inga Khurtsilava (Georgia), GM Ketevan Arakhamia-Grant (Scotland), and Yelena Gaichenya (Kazakhstan). Calzetta Ruiz has made the strongest start, but Cramling is close behind, and the group on 3.5 points is certainly not out of the picture. The next few rounds should give a clearer indication of who will be fighting for the medals. Standings after Round 5 Open 50+: Three Grandmasters share the lead The Open 50+ championship features a particularly strong field, with several experienced grandmasters competing for the title. After four consecutive victories, GMs Petr Kostenko and Kiril Georgiev drew their direct encounter in the fifth round, moving to 4.5 points each. They were joined at the top by GM Pavel Kotsur, who drew with GM Ramil Hasangatin. Georgiev, a former World Junior Champion and one of Bulgaria’s most distinguished grandmasters, remains one of the leading title contenders. A strong chasing group is just half a point behind, including GMs Ramil Hasangatin, Victor Mikhalevski, Hannes Stefansson, Suat Atalik and Mikheil Kekelidze. The top seed, GM Murtas Kazhgaleyev of Kazakhstan, recovered from an earlier setback with a fifth-round victory and stands on 3.5 points. With three players sharing the lead and several experienced grandmasters close behind, the battle for the title remains wide open. Standings after Round 5 Open 65+: Five players tied at the top The Open 65+ championship is developing into a fascinating contest, with five players sharing the lead on 4.5 points after five rounds. The fifth-round encounter between top seed GM Zurab Sturua of Georgia and England’s GM Keith Arkell ended in a draw, leaving both players on 4.5 points. GMs Rainer Knaak of Germany and Branko Damljanović of Serbia joined them at the top after winning their fifth-round games. Knaak defeated Dominique Guigonis, while Damljanović overcame IM David Cummings. IM Oleg Kozlov also moved to 4.5 points following his victory over IM Vladimir Bogdanov, completing a five-way tie for first place. A five-way tie at the top sets the stage for an intriguing second half of the championship, where experience and consistency could make all the difference. The first five rounds have already provided plenty of interesting games and a few surprises, but the most important battles are still ahead. Standings after Round 5 Galina Strutinskaya’s five consecutive victories have been the outstanding individual achievement so far. In the other three categories, the margins at the top are much smaller, leaving several players with realistic hopes of claiming a world title. The FIDE World Senior Chess Championships 2026 continue at Hotel Zepter in Vrnjačka Banja, with the final round scheduled for November 14. Vrnjačka Banja Trophy 2026 rapid chess tournament As part of the World Senior Chess Championship, the international open rapid chess tournament Vrnjačka Banja Trophy 2026 was held on November 8, bringing together 293 participants from 40 countries, including 17 grandmasters. The tournament offered an opportunity for players of different generations to compete against each other, with a significant number of participants from the World Senior Championships also joining the field. Their presence added an interesting dimension to the event, bringing together experienced senior players and younger competitors in a lively and competitive atmosphere. The tournament was opened with a ceremonial first move by Ivana Drenovak, Chief of Staff to the President of the Municipality of Vrnjačka Banja, and Zoran Gajić, Minister of Sports in the technical government. Both, along with Andrija Jorgić, President of the Chess Federation of Serbia, addressed those present. GM Mikhail Bryakin (Serbia) claimed first place with an excellent score of 8/9, finishing ahead of IM Miodrag Perunović (Serbia) and GM Evgeny Vorobiov (Russia), who also scored eight points but were separated by tie-breaks. IM Danila Sutormin (Serbia) finished fourth with 7.5 points, followed by GM Rogelio Antonio Jr. (Philippines) and GM Goran Todorović (Serbia), also on 7.5 points. title: World Junior Blitz Championship 2026: Pranav V and Kleymenova claim titles in Al Ain
summary: Sheikh Sultan bin Khalifa bin Sultan bin Shakhbout Al Nahyan, President of the Asian Chess Federation, Chairman of Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club and Chairman of the Organising Committee, crowned the World Junior Blitz champions at a ceremony held at Danat Al Ain Resort on Friday evening, November 6. The ceremony was attended by FIDE representative Javier Ochoa de Echagüen of Spain, President of the Ibero-American Chess Federation, alongside chess federation presidents, officials and representatives of the participating delegations. The awards ceremony marked the conclusion of the FIDE World Junior Rapid & Blitz Chess Championships 2026, hosted in Al Ain from November 1 to 7 under the patronage of His Highness Sheikh Nahyan bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Chairman of Zayed for Good Foundation and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Sports Council. Organised by Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club in cooperation with the UAE Chess Federation and under the supervision of FIDE, the championships brought together 185 players from 40 countries to compete for four world titles. The medal presentations began with Chief Arbiter Dr Sultan Ali Al Taher being invited to announce the official winners of the World Junior Girls’ Blitz Championship. Valeria Kleymenova (Russia) claimed the under-20 world title and the gold medal with 10 points. Afruza Khamdamova (Uzbekistan) secured silver with 9½ points, while Veronika Iudina (Russia) took bronze with the same score. In the World Junior Under-20 Blitz Championship, Pranav V (India), a World Junior Champion in classical chess, added the world junior blitz title to his achievements, winning gold with 10½ points. Eldiyar Orozbaev (Kyrgyzstan) finished second with 9½ points, while Robert Piliposyan (Armenia) earned bronze with the same score.  Arab players also made their mark, with talented 13-year-old Syrian Mazen Fandi finishing fourth overall with 9½ points, level on points with the silver and bronze medallists. The Indian national anthem was played following the medal presentations.  After the top three players in both sections had received their medals, the ceremony continued with the presentation of special awards. Benard Wanjala, President of the African Chess Confederation, presented the Best Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club Player award to Ghaith Saeed Al Nuaimi, who scored seven points. Zainab Darwish Almaamari received the club’s Best Female Player award with six points. FIDE Technical Delegate Özgür Solakoğlu presented the Best Arab Player award to the UAE’s Rashid Husain Alhammadi, who finished with eight points. Dr Karim Wagih, General Supervisor of Committees at the Egyptian Chess Federation, presented the Best Arab Female Player award to the UAE’s Ahoud Eisa Mohamed, who also scored eight points. The Best Arab Player and Best Arab Female Player awards were introduced to celebrate Al Ain’s designation as the Arab Capital of Tourism for 2026 and to encourage Arab talent to compete on the world stage. Other special award recipients included the UAE’s Mariam Khalifa AlQubaisi, who won the Best Under-12 Female Player award with six points. The event marked the third world championship hosted by Al Ain Chess & Mind Games Club in the city, following the 2012 World Cities Chess Championship for the Sheikh Zayed Cup and the 2013 World Youth Chess Championships. It continued Al Ain’s tradition of staging international and continental events, further strengthening its position as a destination for sport, tourism and culture. Guided by its vision of being “a global community sports institution”, the club continues to combine the organisation of major championships with success at the highest competitive level. Its achievements include winning the Asian Club Championship in 2008 and the World Rapid Team Championship in 2024.

title: Bavarian Championship: Four players finish tied for first, Sasikiran claims title on tiebreaks
summary:
Indian grandmaster Krishnan Sasikiran won the Bavarian Chess Championship in Gmund am Tegernsee, finishing on 7½/9 points and taking first place on tiebreaks. German GMs Frederik Svane and Roven Vogel finished second and third, while Indian FM Arun Daakshin also reached 7½ points. All four won their final-round games with the black pieces, bringing an event that attracted 548 participants to a close. | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Sasikiran, Svane and Vogel reach the podium after exciting final round

Indian GM Krishnan Sasikiran won the 29 th Open International Bavarian Chess Championship, which concluded on Sunday in Gmund am Tegernsee. The nine-round Swiss tournament, held at Gut Kaltenbrunn from 31 October to 8 November, attracted 548 participants.

Sasikiran finished with 7½/9 points, the same score as German GMs Frederik Svane and Roven Vogel and Indian FM Arun Daakshin. The title was decided by the first tiebreak criterion, the average rating of opponents, which favoured Sasikiran. Svane finished second, Vogel third and Daakshin fourth.

The situation atop the standings changed considerably in Saturday's penultimate round, when top seed Svane defeated G.N. Gopal with the white pieces. Alexander Donchenko, Leonardo Costa, Roven Vogel and several other contenders also collected full points, leaving nine players tied for first place on 6½/8 going into the final round. Sasikiran remained among the leaders after drawing with second seed Jaime Santos.

Sunday's decisive encounters produced an unusual result: Black won on each of the top four boards. Sasikiran, playing black against German IM Adrian Gschnitzer on board four, obtained attacking chances on the kingside. His opponent's decision to close the centre on move 20 allowed the Indian GM to build up pressure without facing sufficient counterplay. A blunder on move 25 was met by the refutation: a rook sacrifice on f3. Gschnitzer resigned soon after.

With the best tiebreak score among the leaders, Sasikiran knew that a victory would guarantee him first place regardless of the other results. The 45-year-old from Chennai finished the tournament with a performance rating of 2675.

Adrian Gschnitzer facing Krishnan Sasikiran | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

On the top board, Svane had a rather different experience against Turkish IM Eray Kilic. Playing black in the Exchange Variation of the French Defence, the top seed initially had little to work with in a symmetrical position. Kilic, who needed only a draw to secure his final GM norm, defended accurately for much of the encounter. The game eventually reached a rook endgame in which both players had passed pawns, but Kilic made a mistake in the ensuing pawn race. Svane converted his advantage after 92 moves, securing second place while denying his opponent the norm.

Third place went to 26-year-old German GM Roven Vogel, who defeated compatriot Alexander Donchenko with the black pieces. The players reached a typical King's Indian structure, with white advancing on the queenside and Black seeking counterplay against the king. Donchenko declined a repetition of moves shortly before the time control, despite being short of time. The complications that followed eventually favoured Vogel, a former world under-16 champion, who finished with 7½ points.

The fourth player to reach that score was 17-year-old Indian FM Arun Daakshin. Rated 2341 at the start of the event, Daakshin defeated reigning German champion Leonardo Costa on board three. Costa's ambitious play on the kingside allowed his opponent to establish a strong knight in the centre, while Daakshin subsequently opened lines against the white king on the queenside. The victory gave the Indian youngster fourth place in the final standings.

Arun Daakshin upset Leonardo Costa to climb to shared first place in the final standings! | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Frederik Svane defeated Eray Kilic | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Roven Vogel scored a win over third seed Alexander Donchenko after the latter rejected the chance to get a draw by repetition | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Gopal, who had led outright after round six, recovered from his loss to Svane by defeating American IM Evan Park in the final round. He finished fifth with 7/9 points, ahead of Rithvik Raja, Elham Amar and English IM Sohum Lohia, who also scored 7 points. Donchenko and Costa, meanwhile, ended the tournament with 6½ points following their final-round defeats.

Among the other notable results, Polish IM Klaudia Kulon finished as the highest-placed woman with 6½ points, ahead of German WGM Kateryna Dolzhykova on tiebreaks. Svenja Butenandt took third place in the women's standings with six points and secured a WIM norm after drawing with GM Mathias Womacka in the final round.

Indian youngster S Midilesh M also achieved an IM norm, defeating Georg Seul in the last round to finish on 6½ points. In the senior category, 62-year-old IM Dieter Morawietz took first place on tiebreaks with 6 points, ahead of Mathias Womacka and Martin Forchert.

The top women performers (from left to right): Kateryna Dolzhykova (second place), Klaudia Kulon (first place) and Svenja Butenandt (third place) | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Time to relax | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

But casual chess games go on, of course! | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

title: Yu Yangyi retains Chinese Rapid Championship title after Armageddon decider
summary:
Yu Yangyi successfully defended his Chinese Rapid Championship title in Shaoxing, defeating 18-year-old Xiao Tong in an Armageddon decider after six games had failed to separate the finalists. Xiao had previously eliminated Ding Liren and Lu Shanglei in blitz tiebreaks to reach the final. Meanwhile, Lu secured third place by defeating Xu Xiangyu. | Photo: Chinese Chess Association

A seven-game final

Yu Yangyi successfully defended his title at the fifth Chinese Rapid Championship, held in Shaoxing from 2 to 6 November. The second seed defeated 18-year-old Xiao Tong in an Armageddon decider after their final had finished level following four rapid games and two blitz tiebreakers. Xiao, who had previously eliminated Ding Liren, finished runner-up, while Lu Shanglei took third place after defeating Xu Xiangyu in blitz tiebreaks.

The tournament brought together 24 players in a knockout competition, with eight seeded participants receiving byes into the round of 16. Matches consisted of four rapid games, played at 15 minutes plus a 10-second increment, followed by blitz tiebreaks, with 3 minutes plus 2-second increments, when necessary.

The early rounds went largely according to the seedings, but the quarterfinals saw three of the four rating favourites eliminated. Ding lost to Xiao in blitz, Wang Hao was defeated by Xu Xiangyu, and Bu Xiangzhi fell to Lu Shanglei. Yu was the only player among the top four seeds to reach the semifinals.

In Thursday's semis, Yu Yangyi had little trouble overcoming Xu Xiangyu, winning three consecutive rapid games to secure a 3–0 victory. His opponent in the final was Xiao Tong, who had another lengthy encounter against Lu Shanglei. All four rapid games ended in draws, leaving the players to settle matters in blitz. Xiao eventually prevailed 3½–2½, becoming the first player born in the 2000s to reach the final in the tournament's five editions.

Lu Shanglei (left) was defeated by Xiao Tong in a contested semifinal matchup | Photo: Chinese Chess Association

The title match on Friday began with Xiao taking the lead. Playing black against the defending champion, the 18-year-old scored a win in the opening game. The second encounter was drawn, but Yu struck back with a victory in game three to level the score. A draw in the fourth game left the players tied at 2–2, making blitz tiebreaks necessary.

Yu won the first blitz game, only for Xiao to respond with a victory of his own in the second. The match therefore went to Armageddon, with Yu playing black and enjoying draw odds. The defending champion did not need to rely on that advantage, however, as he went on to win the game outright, delivering checkmate on move 48. The final score was 4–3 in Yu's favour, giving him a second consecutive title.

All games - Yu v. Xiao

Xiao Tong playing black against eventual tournament winner Yu Yangyi | Photo: Chinese Chess Association

The match for third place between Lu Shanglei and Xu Xiangyu also required tiebreaks. Lu won both blitz games to take third place by a 4–2 overall score. Xu, who had knocked out Wang Hao in the quarterfinals, finished fourth.

For Yu, the result completed a successful title defence after he had survived a difficult quarterfinal encounter against Bai Jinshi. Xiao, meanwhile, finished as runner-up despite entering the knockout stage with a rapid rating of 2476, more than 200 points below Yu's 2679. His run included victories over Zeng Chongsheng, Ding Liren and Lu Shanglei, with all three matches decided in blitz tiebreaks.
